text_paragraph_2: A Chinese-flagged fishery patrol vessel operated by a state fishery research institute has run research-pattern grids on both sides of the Guam subsea cable hub for seven weeks. From August 31 to around September 20, it worked a grid east of Guam between the Bulikula and SEA-US cables. After crossing the Guam and CNMI EEZ between September 20 and 22, it began a second grid west of Guam in the Philippine Sea, still running as of September 29. From August 11 to 29, it had conducted similar activity next to the Philippine EEZ. On September 13, it met a Cook Islands-flagged tanker east of Guam for approximately six hours, likely to refuel. AIS has remained on throughout.
text_paragraph_3: This is the first time the vessel has conducted this kind of activity in the region, having previously operated around China and occasionally in the Indian Ocean. The north-to-south legs and repeated slow-speed stops resemble a survey rather than a fishery patrol or a transit. Both grids sit on cable routes landing at Guam, the landing point for 11 subsea cables and a principal link between the U.S. and Asia. The activity fits a wider pattern of Chinese research vessels mapping the seabed around the Philippines, Guam, Hawaii and Wake.

title: Ghana’s Economic Recovery: When Will the Numbers Reach the Kitchen Table?
text_paragraph_1: Ghana’s economy appears to be turning an important corner. Inflation has fallen sharply from the extraordinary levels experienced during the recent economic crisis, economic growth has strengthened, international reserves have improved, and the country has made significant progress in restoring macroeconomic stability.
text_paragraph_2: But there is a question that statistics alone cannot answer: when will the recovery reach the kitchen table?
text_paragraph_3: For the ordinary Ghanaian, economic recovery is not ultimately measured by GDP growth, reserve accumulation or improvements in debt ratios. It is measured by the price of food, electricity and transport; the availability of jobs; the cost of borrowing; the ability of businesses to survive; and whether household income can comfortably meet everyday expenses.

Ghana’s Industrial Ambition Faces the Reality of High Costs, Expensive Credit and Global Competition
text_paragraph_1: Ghana’s ambition to industrialise, modernise agriculture and create sustainable employment for its growing population is both necessary and achievable. But ambition alone will not transform the economy. The country must confront some fundamental obstacles that continue to make local production expensive and weaken the competitiveness of Ghanaian businesses.
text_paragraph_2: Among the most significant challenges are the cost and reliability of electricity. Manufacturing, agro-processing, cold storage and other productive industries depend heavily on affordable and dependable energy. When electricity becomes expensive or unreliable, production costs rise, businesses lose competitiveness and investors become more cautious. The financial difficulties within the energy sector therefore represent more than an electricity problem; they are an industrialisation problem.
text_paragraph_3: Access to affordable capital presents another major obstacle. With commercial lending rates frequently exceeding 25 percent, many Ghanaian businesses simply cannot borrow sustainably to purchase machinery, expand factories, introduce technology or finance working capital. An entrepreneur may have a viable business idea and a ready market but still find expansion impossible because the cost of borrowing destroys the economics of the investment.

95% of Tanzania’s Employment Is Informal. Can Vision 2050 Reverse It?
text_paragraph_1: About 95% of Tanzania’s employment is informal, while Vision 2050 targets at least 50% of Tanzanians holding decent formal jobs. Reaching that target will require a major transformation of firms, skills, agriculture and labour productivity.
text_paragraph_2: Tanzania has set one of the most ambitious labour market targets in its development history: by 2050, at least 50% of Tanzanians should hold decent jobs in the formal sector. The starting point is far more difficult than the target suggests. The World Bank’s latest Tanzania Economic Update: Making Jobs Work estimates that informality increased from about 93% of employment in 2020 to roughly 95% in 2024 as the working age population expanded faster than the formal job base. Tanzania therefore enters Vision 2050 with an economy in which work is widespread, but formal employment remains the exception.
text_paragraph_3: The target itself is explicit in the government’s Tanzania Development Vision 2050 . Under the goal of improving quality of life and wellbeing, Tanzania aims for at least half of its population to hold decent formal sector jobs by mid century. The same Vision expects Tanzania to become a $1 trillion upper middle income economy with per capita income of $7,000. Formal employment is therefore not a peripheral social target. It sits inside the economic model Tanzania has chosen for becoming substantially richer.

title: Tanzania’s Growth Gains Need Better Jobs to Bring Lasting Prosperity to More Families
text_paragraph_1: Tanzania's economy is expanding, but its next development challenge is ensuring that growth delivers better livelihoods. The World Bank's latest Tanzania Economic Update, featuring "Making Jobs Work", reports GDP growth of 5.9% in 2025 and forecasts expansion of 6.1% in 2026 and 6.5% over the medium term. Yet with nearly 69% of working-age people employed, inadequate earnings remain a concern. The policy challenge is to increase productivity and improve the quality of employment.
text_paragraph_2: For government, businesses and development partners, this means looking beyond headline growth. Progress will depend on whether firms can expand, farmers can earn more and workers can access opportunities that provide a better living.
text_paragraph_3: Finance, trade and transport have been major contributors to economic expansion, alongside increased government spending ahead of the October 2025 elections. However, growth in these activities does not automatically improve earnings for people working in low-productivity agriculture or informal enterprises.

Why Tanzania’s 6% Growth Is Barely Reducing Poverty
text_paragraph_1: Tanzania has averaged 5.7% economic growth for two decades and is projected to grow 6.1% in 2026. Yet poverty has barely moved since 2018 and real private consumption per person grew only 0.2% annually between 2018 and 2025. The World Bank’s latest report explains why productivity is now the central economic challenge.
text_paragraph_2: Tanzania has spent much of the past two decades among Africa’s faster growing economies, averaging about 5.7% real GDP growth a year. The World Bank expects growth to reach 6.1% in 2026 and average around 6.5% over the medium term. Yet its latest Tanzania Economic Update: Making Jobs Work presents a much less comfortable measure of economic progress: the share of Tanzanians living below the $4.20 a day poverty line is estimated at 69.8% in 2026, barely below 70% in 2018, while real private consumption per person increased by an average of only 0.2% a year between 2018 and 2025. Tanzania is producing considerably more economic output, but that expansion is translating into household welfare far more slowly than the headline growth rate would suggest.  World Bank
text_paragraph_3: The World Bank does not argue that Tanzania’s growth is artificial. The economy expanded by 5.9% in 2025, inflation remained within the Bank of Tanzania’s 3% to 5% target range, domestic revenue exceeded budget projections and public debt remained moderate at about 49% of GDP. These are meaningful macroeconomic strengths. The report instead raises a more difficult question about the quality of growth. Tanzania has generated activity, investment and employment, but productivity gains have been insufficient to produce equally strong improvements in incomes. The Bank says growth over the past two decades has been driven primarily by accumulation of resources rather than productivity advances, while productive employment, agricultural productivity and human capital have yet to shift sufficiently to change the poverty trajectory. Why Tanzania Has East Africa’s Most Resilient Debt
text_paragraph_1: Tanzania has the strongest debt resilience among Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda when debt levels, IMF risk assessments and shock absorption capacity are compared. Its debt remains below 50% of GDP, with moderate distress risk and some space to absorb shocks.
text_paragraph_2: Among East Africa’s four major established economies, Tanzania currently enters the next investment cycle with the strongest debt resilience. IMF data put Tanzania’s general government debt at around 49% of GDP, below Uganda at roughly 54%, Rwanda at about 65% and Kenya close to 70%. The difference becomes more significant when debt sustainability assessments are added to the comparison. Tanzania is assessed at moderate risk of debt distress with some space to absorb shocks. Uganda and Rwanda are also at moderate risk, but both have only limited space to absorb shocks, while Kenya remains at high risk of debt distress. On the combination of debt stock, risk classification and shock absorption capacity, Tanzania currently has the most comfortable sovereign debt position among the four economies.
text_paragraph_3: That does not mean Tanzania has low debt in an absolute sense, nor does it give the country unlimited room to borrow. Public debt has risen considerably over the past decade as Tanzania financed railways, electricity generation, roads, airports and other infrastructure. The financing mix is also changing, with greater use of less concessional sources creating higher interest and refinancing exposure than traditional development finance. Tanzania’s advantage is narrower but important: it has undertaken a large infrastructure programme without yet moving into the same degree of debt vulnerability now visible elsewhere in East Africa.

text_paragraph_1: Women’s empowerment is a question of both individual human rights and social progress. As  the United Nations Development Programme (2014) asserts, “Unless women and girls are able  to fully realise their rights in all spheres of life, human development will not be advanced.”
text_paragraph_2: In São Tomé and Príncipe, the government has taken impressive steps to provide a  framework for gender equality, starting with constitutional guarantees since 1975 of women’s  right to own and inherit property and get a job without a husband’s permission (Beeram,  2025). A wide range of legal reforms, policies, strategies, and government entities – including  a Ministry of Women’s Rights – have advanced women’s empowerment since then. Among  milestones are a 2008 law on domestic and family violence and a 2022 law reserving at least  40% of elective and cabinet seats for women (Martins & Corminales, 2022; Groussard, Ferraz  di Ricco, & Martins, 2023; Overvest, 2022).

text_paragraph_2: On September 16, 2026, the Central Bank of The Gambia (CBG) sent a letter titled “Directive on the Recruitment of Non-Gambian Staff” to the MDs of all banks. So you know, there are 11 banks in The Gambia and four are subsidiaries of Nigerian banking groups: Access Bank, FirstBank, Guaranty Trust Bank and one other. Africa’s Highest Debt: Sudan, Senegal and Mozambique
text_paragraph_1: Sudan’s debt stands at 187.6% of GDP, Senegal’s at 130.2% and Mozambique remains above the danger line. Their ratios look similar, but war, hidden liabilities, arrears and financing structures have created three very different African debt problems.
text_paragraph_2: Africa’s debt problem is not evenly distributed. The continental debt to GDP ratio may have eased from its recent peak, but several countries remain far outside the African norm. IMF data for 2025 place Sudan’s general government gross debt at 187.6% of GDP and Senegal’s at 130.2%, while the October 2026 debt map places Mozambique above 100%. These are not three versions of the same fiscal problem. Sudan’s ratio sits inside a war damaged economy whose GDP has collapsed. Senegal’s debt was dramatically revised upward after previously undisclosed liabilities were uncovered. Mozambique’s problem combines a heavy public debt burden with arrears, expensive domestic borrowing and an IMF assessment that overall public debt remains in distress. The ratios look similar because they are all exceptionally high. The economics behind them are very different.
text_paragraph_3: That difference matters because debt to GDP is often interpreted as if it were a direct measure of fiscal failure. It is not. The ratio can rise because debt increases, because GDP falls, because previously hidden liabilities are added to the official stock, because a currency depreciates against foreign debt, or because several of these forces occur at the same time. Sudan, Senegal and Mozambique show why Africa’s highest debt ratios have to be analysed through the history of how the debt was accumulated and the capacity of the economy to service it.

Morocco’s Elections in a Time of Despotism: Why Ballot Boxes Don’t Produce Liberation
text_paragraph_1: Einstein defined insanity as repeating the same experiment with the same tools under the same conditions while expecting different results. Today, I believe that Morocco is experiencing a form of political insanity in the Einsteinian sense. The elections on September 23 showcased the same familiar faces that have worn thin on the Moroccan public, accompanied by the same broken promises and poorly executed theatrics. Furthermore, it is the Ministry of the Interior that oversees the entire electoral process—from drawing constituency maps to organising the vote itself. Despite these circumstances, both old and new mouthpieces of power persist in trying to persuade us of the necessity of participating in this appointment to construct a new Morocco with the same old system. It is as if the sheer number of electoral lists could create genuine pluralism: 28 parties, 1,850 lists, 7,288 candidates—more than 18 candidates per seat—yet the political offerings remain fundamentally poor and largely unchanged.
text_paragraph_2: Contrary to what various forms of disinformation would have us believe, we are not voting in an imperfect democracy that merely needs “improvement”. We are voting in an absolute despotic system in which legislative, executive, and judicial powers are effectively concentrated in the hands of the king and his advisors—what might be called the real shadow government: unelected, unaccountable, and absent from any electoral platform. Parliament legislates only within the margin it is allowed. The government carries out decisions made elsewhere. The judiciary has only as much independence as it is granted. In this context, political parties do not compete to serve citizens; rather, they vie for a better position within the system by presenting themselves as the most capable of implementing the neoliberal policies that are devastating social and economic rights, the most skilled at “managing” popular anger, and the most devoted to advising the regime on how to prevent the next uprising. The winning party is not the one that wins voters but the one that convinces those above it that it can absorb the shock and delay the explosion. Nothing illustrates the situation better than the declarations heads of government routinely make upon taking office: that their essential mission is the literal execution of the royal agenda.
text_paragraph_3: These are rotten parties, in the direct moral and political sense of the word, given the involvement of several of their leaderships in financial and administrative corruption scandals—and rotten in the figurative sense too, meaning that their shelf life (périmé) has expired. They are no longer even fit for the role they were created to play: camouflaging authoritarianism and lending legitimacy to a fictitious multiparty system that functions, in practice, much closer to a single-party model, despite the multiplicity of names and symbols.

text_paragraph_2: Africa’s debt problem is not evenly distributed. The continental debt to GDP ratio may have eased from its recent peak, but several countries remain far outside the African norm. IMF data for 2025 place Sudan’s general government gross debt at 187.6% of GDP and Senegal’s at 130.2%, while the October 2026 debt map places Mozambique above 100%. These are not three versions of the same fiscal problem. Sudan’s ratio sits inside a war damaged economy whose GDP has collapsed. Senegal’s debt was dramatically revised upward after previously undisclosed liabilities were uncovered. Mozambique’s problem combines a heavy public debt burden with arrears, expensive domestic borrowing and an IMF assessment that overall public debt remains in distress. The ratios look similar because they are all exceptionally high. The economics behind them are very different.
text_paragraph_3: That difference matters because debt to GDP is often interpreted as if it were a direct measure of fiscal failure. It is not. The ratio can rise because debt increases, because GDP falls, because previously hidden liabilities are added to the official stock, because a currency depreciates against foreign debt, or because several of these forces occur at the same time. Sudan, Senegal and Mozambique show why Africa’s highest debt ratios have to be analysed through the history of how the debt was accumulated and the capacity of the economy to service it.

text_paragraph_1: MATI today released El Niño: Voices of the Farmers, a field report available at el-nino.maticarbon.com, gathering first-hand accounts from smallholder farmers in India and Zambia on how the 2026 growing season unfolded under a strengthening El Niño. The report is published during Climate Week NYC and the high-level week of the United Nations General Assembly, where the effect of climate disruption on food systems is a central topic, and where the farmers most exposed to it are rarely heard directly. In September 2026, as forecasters upgraded the current El Niño to very strong, MATI asked farmers in both countries three questions: what changed in the weather this year, what it did to the farm and the family, and what they expect next year. The report carries each farmer's answers, in Hindi, English or Chitonga, with the recordings where they survive and a photograph taken at the interview. These are individual accounts rather than a survey, and they do not all agree with one another. MATI has published them as given.
text_paragraph_2: "Farmers are the first to see what a changing climate does to a harvest, and they are the last to be asked about it," said Shantanu Agarwal, CEO of MATI. "This El Niño has not yet reached its peak, and farmers in India are already describing a season that cost them money before it cost them yield. We are publishing their accounts so that the people meeting in New York this week can hear directly from the people whose livelihoods are on the line."
text_paragraph_3: El Niño is a periodic warming of the central and eastern Pacific that shifts rainfall patterns across much of the world. Its historical signature in the two regions covered by the report is well documented: a weaker and less reliable Indian summer monsoon, and dry conditions across southern Africa during the main rains on which Zambian maize depends. In its September 10, 2026 update, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center gave a greater than 90 percent chance of a very strong event through autumn and winter, and a 75 percent chance that October to December runs stronger than any El Niño on record back to 1950. Forecasters expect it to keep building through the end of 2026 and run into 2027. What the farmers in this report describe happened under an El Niño that was still strengthening. The season they are preparing for is the one ahead.

text_paragraph_1: Now the country is trying to reverse this trajectory. Argane planted 80 tree seedlings on his farmland and another 50 in a communal area — a small contribution to a vastly larger effort. As soils lost their fertility, cultivation moved onto increasingly marginal land, including steep slopes, where tillage and the loss of protective vegetation led to the erosion of fertile topsoil, which washed into rivers and reservoirs. By 1989, forest cover was estimated at less than 3 percent , while Ethiopia’s highlands were losing around 1 billion metric tons of topsoil every year.

text_paragraph_1: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, queer/questioning, transgender, intersex and asexual/ace (LGBTQIA+) people face acute risks in everyday life, and these risks are compounded and exacerbated by the onset of armed violence. These harms also intersect with other forms of marginalisation on the basis of socioeconomic background, age, migration status, racialisation, disability and other axes of oppression.
text_paragraph_2: However, major gaps and failures characterise the international sector’s efforts at inclusion to date – gaps that could be eased if LGBTQIA+ civil society organisations (CSOs) were treated as true partners in terms of programme design, humanitarian access, funding, coordination and decision-making power. In the face of significant cuts and attacks on diversity and inclusion since early 2025, these gaps are only widening – and addressing them is more important than it has ever been before.
text_paragraph_3: This briefing note draws on primary research undertaken in 2025 and 2026 by The PRIDE Centre: Protection, Rights, Inclusion in Displacement & Emergencies, which took place in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Ethiopia and Nigeria, and by the Humanitarian Policy Group (HPG) in Haiti and Syria. Across these contexts, our research reveals diversity as well as synchronicity – that is, while important common threads can be found across the settings under study, they also show profound diversity and specificity, which serves as a further argument for consultation and coordination with place-based actors as experts.

text_paragraph_2: “I didn’t even know my child was malnourished,” says Farhiya’s mother, Hawo, adding, “I hope I can get the support I need for my child to recover.” (As a displaced person, Hawo’s last name is being withheld for her protection).

text_paragraph_1: Sandeep Walia’s career has developed inside one company, but not inside one market or one type of hotel. Since joining Marriott International in 2005, he has moved through finance, development and operational leadership, building a perspective that connects owner returns, brand standards and the daily realities of hotel teams. Walia has more than 25 years of international hospitality experience. He became chief operating officer for Marriott’s Middle East business in 2021 and added responsibility for luxury operations across Europe, the Middle East and Africa in 2024. In 2026, his remit expanded again to include sub-Saharan Africa and global leadership of Design Hotels, the collection of independent, design-led properties affiliated with Marriott.
text_paragraph_2: The numbers explain the management challenge. Walia oversees more than 410 hotels and around 90,000 rooms across a region that includes mature tourism capitals, fast-growing Gulf markets, resort destinations and African cities with very different infrastructure and demand. Marriott opened 35 properties with about 6,500 rooms in the region during 2025 and is targeting significant additional growth in Africa. Saudi Arabia is a major engine. A 10-hotel agreement valued at about $1.33 billion illustrates how Marriott is using multiple brands to match new destinations and customer segments. Across the Gulf, the company is expanding luxury, select-service and extended-stay offerings while competing for owners with every major global group. Walia’s role is therefore as much about relationships as hotel operations. Marriott generally grows through management and franchise agreements, so owners provide the capital and expect performance. The operator must protect brand standards while adapting to local project economics. Walia’s grounding in finance helps him understand that tension, while his operational career keeps the guest and associate experience in view.
text_paragraph_3: He has consistently argued for a people-first model. Hospitality growth in the region is creating intense competition for general managers, chefs, commercial leaders and frontline teams. Recruitment alone will not solve it. Training, mobility, local career pathways and inclusive leadership determine whether new hotels can deliver the service promised by their brands. Luxury adds another layer. Travellers increasingly expect personalisation, cultural connection and distinctive design rather than uniform formality. Walia must manage established flags such as Ritz-Carlton, St. Regis and JW Marriott while giving Design Hotels’ independent members room to preserve their identity. Scale creates distribution and loyalty benefits, but too much standardisation can erase the qualities that make a property desirable.
